key_terms.meaning: A live view of the real world with computer-made 3D objects added and kept fixed to real places.
Keeping a virtual object aligned with its real object or place in 3D as the camera or user moves.
Updating pose and display fast enough that virtual objects do not visibly lag behind motion.
The user sees the real world directly through a combiner, and virtual light is added to that view.
A camera captures the real scene, and virtual objects are mixed into the camera pixels on a screen.
A semi-transparent optical element that lets real light pass while adding virtual light to the eye.
A thin optical element that guides virtual light inside glass or plastic and sends it to the eye.
A projector throws virtual light directly onto a real surface, so no headset is needed.
A printed pattern with known geometry that a camera detects to compute its pose.
Pose estimation from natural image features or objects instead of a printed marker.
Simultaneous localization and mapping: the camera builds a map while estimating its own pose in that map.
A fixed point in the real world to which a toolkit attaches virtual content.
An image or object that an AR toolkit is trained to detect and track.
A set of targets stored on the device for offline detection and tracking.
A set of targets stored on a server and queried over a network by the AR app.
A file holding a camera's intrinsic parameters, such as focal length, principal point and distortion.
Motion estimation that fuses camera images with inertial sensor data from an IMU.
The direction of the eyes or head used as a pointing or selection input in mixed reality.
A recognised hand pose or motion used as a command in mixed reality.
The time from a user motion to the display showing updated photons for that motion.

takeaways: AR has three hard requirements: combine real and virtual, register in 3D, and run live.
Optical see-through sends real light and virtual light to the eye, while video see-through sends both as pixels to a screen.
Projection AR sends virtual light directly onto a real surface and is useful for hands-free shared views.
Tracking is chosen by how much known structure the scene gives: a printed marker, natural features, or a SLAM map.
An AR toolkit hides tracking behind target or anchor calls that return a pose in every frame.
Mixed reality interaction is multimodal and needs confirmation plus feedback inside a frame or two.
AR earns its cost where information belongs to a place or object: a patient, a machine, a page, or a street.
The metaverse needs persistence, shared synchrony, low motion-to-photon latency, wearable optics and portable APIs such as OpenXR.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to compare display routes and tracking families, explain toolkit pose flow, and connect interaction limits to real applications and XR trends.

bank.q: Define augmented reality. Explain the three requirements of an AR system and contrast AR with VR using one example each.
outline: Clear definition of AR as live real world plus registered virtual objects
Three requirements: combine real and virtual, register in 3D, run in real time
AR vs VR: real world visible in AR, fully synthetic world in VR
Examples such as phone AR furniture placement vs VR training room

bank.q: Explain optical see-through and video see-through AR displays. Compare what reaches the eye, brightness, latency and occlusion, and state where projection AR fits.
outline: OST: real light direct, virtual light added by combiner or waveguide
VST: camera captures real scene, virtual pixels mixed on screen
Compare brightness, camera latency, field of view and occlusion handling
Projection AR: virtual light sent onto real surface, no headset

bank.q: Explain marker-based, markerless and SLAM tracking. State the assumption each makes and give one use case for each.
outline: Marker-based: printed fiducial with known geometry
Markerless: natural features or known images
SLAM: map built while camera moves; pose estimated in that map
Use cases: manual page, product box, room-scale walkthrough

bank.q: Describe the pose flow in an AR toolkit: target or anchor, device or cloud database, camera calibration and VIO, and the pose returned each frame.
outline: App declares a target image or a real-world anchor
Device database works offline; cloud database needs network
Camera calibration supplies intrinsics for pose computation
VIO fuses camera and IMU; toolkit returns pose every frame

bank.q: Design an AR human anatomy learning app for a phone. Choose the display route, tracking method, toolkit features and interaction, and justify each choice.
outline: Handheld video see-through is practical on a phone
Marker or image target for a printed body chart; markerless or SLAM for room-scale model
Toolkit needs target detection, anchors and camera calibration
Interaction: tap, drag, pinch, voice labels; feedback for selection

bank.q: Design an AR maintenance guide for a factory machine. Explain how to anchor labels to parts, handle tracking loss, and give feedback for hand and voice commands.
outline: Use markerless or SLAM tracking with anchors on machine parts
Store target data on device for weak network areas
Tracking loss: freeze label, show warning, re-localise
Hand and voice commands need confirmation and visible feedback

bank.q: Plan an AR walkthrough of a historic place. Compare handheld video see-through with spatial projection, choose marker or SLAM tracking, and describe navigation aids.
outline: Handheld VST gives private view; projection gives shared public view
Marker for fixed plaques; SLAM for open outdoor movement
Navigation: map, arrows, audio cues and wayfinding anchors
Evaluate sunlight, surface brightness and tracking drift

bank.q: A team wants AR surgery simulation. Select display, tracking and latency targets; say why VR alone is insufficient and where AR helps.
outline: OST or VST choice with reasons for surgery training
Tracking must be stable and registered to a phantom or patient model
Low motion-to-photon latency and clear occlusion needs
AR keeps real patient or phantom visible; VR gives full synthetic control

bank.q: Analyse the main causes of bad registration in AR: drift, jitter and occlusion. Suggest display and tracking fixes for each.
outline: Drift: pose error accumulates; fix with SLAM relocalisation or markers
Jitter: noisy pose; fix with filtering, VIO and stable anchors
Occlusion: virtual objects draw over real ones; fix with depth sensing or VST masking
Display choice affects how easily errors are seen

bank.q: Evaluate gaze, hand gesture, voice and controller input for mixed reality. Explain confirmation and feedback needs for each.
outline: Gaze is fast for pointing but needs dwell or confirmation
Hand gestures are natural but tiring and error-prone
Voice is good for commands but needs privacy and error handling
Controllers are precise; all modes need visible or audio feedback

bank.q: Evaluate the metaverse as a persistent shared 3D layer. Discuss AR cloud, motion-to-photon latency, wearable optics and OpenXR portability.
outline: Persistence and shared synchrony define the metaverse layer
AR cloud stores shared real-world maps
Latency and comfort limit always-on wearables
OpenXR reduces device fragmentation; hardware trends make XR lighter

bank.q: AR is worth its cost where information belongs to a place or object. Evaluate this claim using medicine, education, entertainment and industry examples.
outline: Criterion: information tied to a patient, page, stage or machine
Medicine: overlay on patient or model; education: overlay on book or lab kit
Entertainment: place-based games and try-before-buy
Industry: machine repair and remote guidance; compare where VR is better

bank.q: Compare Vuforia, ARCore and ARKit as AR toolkits: what they track, device bases, databases and calibration. Choose one for a classroom AR app and justify.
outline: Vuforia: strong image and object targets, device and cloud databases
ARCore and ARKit: phone platform tracking with anchors and VIO
Compare device coverage, calibration needs and offline support
Classroom choice depends on phones available and target type

glossary.def: A live real-world view with computer-made objects registered to real places.
A system where real and virtual objects coexist and interact in one registered 3D space.
Alignment of virtual content with the real world in three dimensions.
A display route where real light reaches the eye directly and virtual light is added.
A display route where cameras capture the real scene and a screen shows real and virtual pixels together.
A semi-transparent optical part that overlays virtual light on the direct real view.
A thin light-guide that carries virtual display light to the eye in AR glasses.
AR made by projecting virtual light onto a real surface rather than wearing a display.
A printed pattern with known size and shape used for camera pose estimation.
Tracking from natural features, images or objects instead of a printed marker.
A method that estimates camera pose while building a map of the unknown environment.
A real-world point or plane to which virtual content is attached by a toolkit.
An image or object that an AR toolkit is trained to recognise and track.
A local store of AR targets that works without a network connection.
A remote store of AR targets that the app queries over a network.
A file of camera intrinsics and distortion values used to compute correct pose.
Camera plus IMU motion estimation used to track a device smoothly.
Eye or head direction used as an input signal in mixed reality.
A hand pose or movement recognised as a command.
Interaction that combines inputs such as gaze, voice, gesture and controllers.
The delay between user motion and the matching updated image on the display.
A persistent, shared, synchronous 3D layer over the internet.
A shared cloud map of the real world used to place persistent multi-user AR content.
A folded optical design using polarisation to make VR and MR headsets thinner.
A display technology using tiny light-emitting diodes per pixel for bright, low-power screens.
An open standard API that lets XR software run on different devices and runtimes.
